results.question: What happens if a Thief fails an Open Locks attempt?
results.expected: The Thief must wait until gaining another level of experience before trying again. It may only be tried once per lock.
results.agent_answer: If a Thief fails an Open Locks attempt, they cannot try that particular lock again until they have gained at least one additional level of experience. This is to reflect the meaningful consequences of failure in the Thief abilities. The Game Master may also rule that the failed attempt has triggered the trap, depending on the nature of the trap.

chunks.text: Open Locks: A Thief may attempt to open a lock given a set of thieves' picks and tools. The base chance of success is shown on the Thief Abilities table and improves with each level gained. To attempt to pick a lock, the Thief rolls percentile dice (d%); if the result is equal to or less than the listed percentage, the attempt succeeds and the lock opens. A Thief may only make one attempt per lock. If the attempt fails, the Thief may not try that particular lock again until he or she has gained at least one additional level of experience. It is important to note that magically held locks — such as those secured by Hold Portal or Wizard Lock — cannot be picked by a Thief at all; only the caster of the spell or a Dispel Magic can undo such locks. Normal locks, padlocks, and chest locks all fall within the scope of this ability. The Game Master may impose penalties to the roll for particularly complex or well-made locks, or grant bonuses for simple or cheap ones.

Remove Traps: A Thief may attempt to disarm a trap once the trap has been located (typically through the Find Traps ability). The Thief rolls percentile dice and compares the result to the listed chance on the Thief Abilities table. Unlike Open Locks, a Thief may make up to two attempts to remove a particular trap. If the first attempt fails, the Thief may try once more. If both attempts fail, the Thief cannot try again until gaining at least one additional level of experience, in the same manner as failed Open Locks attempts. Additionally, on a failed second attempt, the GM may rule that the trap has been triggered by the bungled removal effort — the probability of this is up to the GM's judgment based on the trap's nature. This limitation on retries is consistent with the broader design of Thief abilities: failure has meaningful consequences, and advancement in level is the only path to a second chance.

Thieves have a number of special abilities that set them apart from other character classes. These abilities improve as the Thief gains levels, as shown on the Thief Abilities table. The abilities are: Open Locks, Remove Traps, Pick Pockets, Move Silently, Climb Walls, Hide, and Listen. Percentile dice (d%) are rolled and the result compared against the listed percentage chance. For most abilities, a roll equal to or less than the listed percentage indicates success. Thieves using these abilities should generally do so secretly, with the Game Master rolling the dice and informing the player only of the outcome — not the roll itself — where appropriate. This preserves tension and prevents a player from knowing with certainty whether a trap has been properly disarmed or whether a pickpocketing attempt was detected. The Thief class represents the quintessential rogue archetype: skilled, stealthy, and opportunistic. Thieves wear leather armor and may use swords, daggers, and other light weapons. They advance using the Thief attack bonus table and use a d6 for hit points.

Fighters use a d8 for hit points, but the Elf does not gain the Fighter's hardier constitution — the trade-off for broader capabilities is a reduced hit die. The inability to roll higher than a d6 for hit points is therefore a direct consequence of the Elf being a combination class — it is the class's defined hit die, not a racial penalty.

results.question: Can a character wear leather armor and cast spells?
results.expected: Magic-Users and Elves cannot cast spells while wearing armor. Clerics can wear armor and cast spells.
results.agent_answer:
A character cannot wear leather armor and cast spells simultaneously. According to the Basic Fantasy RPG rulebook:

1. Magic-Users and Elves cannot cast spells while wearing any type of armor, including leather armor.
2. Clerics, on the other hand, can wear any type of armor and cast spells without restriction.

Therefore, a character wearing leather armor would not be able to cast spells.

chunks.text: Magic-Users may not wear armor of any type. This restriction applies at all times — a Magic-User cannot cast spells while wearing armor, and indeed may not wear armor even in situations where no spellcasting is planned. Elves share the restriction on casting spells in armor: an Elf wearing armor of any kind, including leather armor, cannot cast spells. An Elf may, however, choose to wear armor on a given day and simply not cast spells, or choose to go unarmored and cast freely — but the two cannot coexist in the same moment. This restriction applies to all arcane spellcasters and is not modified by armor type; leather armor imposes the same prohibition as plate mail. Clerics are a notable exception: they may wear any armor, including heavy armor and shields, and still cast their divine spells without restriction. Clerics are the only spellcasting class with no armor-related casting limitation.

Clerics may wear any type of armor and may carry shields. This is a significant advantage over the other spellcasting classes: unlike Magic-Users and Elves, Clerics suffer no restriction on casting spells while armored. A Cleric in full plate mail prays for spells and casts them in exactly the same way as a Cleric in robes would. However, Clerics are restricted in the weapons they may use. By the tenets of their religious calling, Clerics are forbidden from using edged or pointed weapons — weapons designed to cut or pierce. Clerics may use blunt weapons such as maces, war hammers, flails, and clubs. Clerics may also use slings for ranged combat. The prohibition against edged and pointed weapons applies regardless of the deity served; it is a universal feature of the Cleric class as presented in Basic Fantasy RPG. This means Clerics cannot use swords, daggers, spears, or bows. This weapon limitation is the primary trade-off for the Cleric's freedom to wear armor and cast divine spells without restriction.

Elves are a combination class, having the abilities of both Fighters and Magic-Users. An Elf may fight in melee, wear armor, use any weapon, and also memorize and cast spells from the Magic-User spell list. However, an Elf may not cast spells while wearing armor of any kind — this includes leather armor. An Elf who wishes to cast spells must do so unarmored. In a given adventure, an Elf may fight in armor on some days and cast spells unarmored on other days, but cannot do both simultaneously. The weapons, armor, and other equipment available to an Elf are otherwise the same as those available to Fighters. Elves begin play able to memorize a single 1st-level spell. results.question: What is the difference between a retainer and a hireling?
results.expected: Retainers are NPCs who accompany the party on adventures and gain experience. Hirelings are hired for specific non-adventuring tasks.
results.agent_answer:
A retainer in Basic Fantasy RPG is an NPC who travels with and adventures alongside player characters on a long-term basis. They fight, explore dungeons, and face danger as active members of the party. Retainers gain experience points for their participation in adventures and will advance in level over time, just as player characters do. A character's Charisma score determines both the maximum number of retainers that character may employ simultaneously and those retainers' base morale score. Retainers expect a share of treasure in addition to a regular wage.

On the other hand, hirelings are employees hired to perform specific, typically non-adventuring tasks. They do not accompany the party into dungeons or combat situations. Hirelings are tradespeople and specialists such as armorers, sages, engineers, ship's crew, or common laborers who perform a defined job for a set wage. Hirelings do not earn experience points, do not receive shares of treasure, and are not expected to risk their lives.

In summary, the key difference is that retainers are adventuring companions, while hirelings are service workers.

results.question: When can a Magic-User learn new spells?

These newly added spells are assumed to have been researched and learned through continued study between adventures.

2. **External Sources**: Magic-Users may learn spells from other sources such as scrolls discovered during adventures or spell books from other Magic-Users encountered in play. However, adding spells from external sources is subject to the Game Master's discretion and may require the Magic-User to spend time, money, or other resources to successfully copy and learn a spell.

3. **Spell Book**: Every Magic-User maintains a spell book, a handwritten record of all the spells they have learned. Without access to the spell book, a Magic-User cannot memorize new instances of their spells after resting. If the spell book is lost, the Magic-User must reconstruct it by finding and copying spells from scrolls, other spell books, or through research and practice.

Medium weapons may be used by Halflings, but must be wielded two-handed rather than one-handed; a Halfling using a sword, for example, must use both hands to wield it effectively. Small weapons such as daggers are used normally by Halflings with no restriction. Because the longbow is classified as a Large weapon, a Halfling cannot use it under any circumstances. Halflings wishing to use a bow must rely on the shortbow, which is a Medium weapon and therefore available to Halflings when wielded two-handed. This restriction means that despite their racial bonus to missile attack rolls, Halflings are limited in which ranged weapons they may employ.

Halflings are small demi-humans standing about 3 feet tall and typically weighing around 60 pounds. Despite their small size, they are surprisingly capable adventurers with several notable racial abilities. In outdoor settings — rural terrain, forests, fields — a Halfling not wearing metal armor can attempt to Hide with a base 90% chance of success, a substantially better rate than most characters. Halflings also receive a +1 bonus to all missile attack rolls, reflecting their exceptional hand-eye coordination and natural aptitude with thrown and ranged weapons. Additionally, Halflings receive a +1 bonus to all saving throws, making them slightly more resistant to a wide variety of dangers. Their small stature, however, places restrictions on the weapons and armor they can use; in particular, Halflings may not use Large weapons such as the longbow or two-handed sword. Halflings use a d6 for hit points, the same die as Clerics, Thieves, and Elves, and they advance using their own attack bonus and saving throw tables.

Missile weapons are ranged weapons that include bows, crossbows, slings, and thrown weapons. Each missile weapon has three range increments — short, medium, and long — that determine accuracy modifiers. Attacks made against a target within short range receive a +1 bonus to the attack roll. Attacks at medium range are made with no modifier. Attacks at long range are made with a –1 penalty. The longbow is one of the most powerful missile weapons available: it has a range of 70 feet (short), 140 feet (medium), and 210 feet (long), and deals 1d6 damage. The shortbow has a shorter range of 50/100/150 feet and also deals 1d6 damage. Both bows fire once per round. Crossbows have greater range than shortbows but typically fire more slowly. The longbow requires two hands to use and is classified as a Large weapon, which has implications for which character races may wield it.
